speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, of which I have given him notice. subtopic: HUNGARIAN REFUGEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that statement is substantially correct. speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, January 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. R. F. L. Hanna for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am happy to join members on both sides of the house, Mr. Speaker, in congratulating the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Apart from the interesting subject matter and the eloquent delivery of the speeches, I was particularly struck by the fact that Canadians from different ethnic groups addressed the house in both official languages. In my opinion the effort made by these hon. members, as well as by many hon, members on both sides of the house, to master both the official languages of our country, is the best guarantee and the best proof that Canada can and will become truly bilingual. I feel also, Mr. Speaker, that if we use all the means at our disposal for keeping the respective languages and cultures and traditions in their purest possible form, then a richer and more profound Canadian culture embodying the best of both ethnic groups can and will evolve.
For almost a year now, Mr. Speaker, it has been my great privilege to work relatively closely with the Department of External Affairs and to study and observe, perhaps more closely than I would otherwise have done, the extraordinary evolution that has taken place in the world over the last half century. As a result of this evolution, there has arisen a greater interdependence amongst states and from this has equally arisen a totally new concept of what international relations must be if the world is to continue to exist and world peace is to be achieved. This concept of modern international relationships has been clearly written in the charter of the United Nations which, as you know, has been signed and ratified by some 80 nations in the world.
The Address-Mr. Cardin
Personally, I am convinced that in spite of the weaknesses that are attributed to the United Nations, international conflicts even at this time can best be resolved and world peace accomplished through the medium of a body which is relatively independent and collectively free of any particular interest in the different international issues at stake. As hon. members know the United Nations charter prevents it from using the authority and the power that it might require to solve international problems effectively and quickly. The granting of much greater power and much greater authority to the United Nations could be interpreted as a step towards world government. Perhaps the time has not yet come to take such a step, and yet perhaps the time is rapidly approaching when such a step will have to be taken.
Two things strike me very forcibly in looking back over the events of late 1956, and in which perhaps we can foresee things to come. The first of these is the unprecedented power and strength of world opinion, so forcibly expressed at the United Nations not so long ago. The second is the accompanying general feeling of despair and indignation because the world was made to witness, and is still being made to witness, horrible crimes committed by the U.S.S.R. in Hungary without being able to lift a finger to stop the atrocious crime of genocide against the Hungarians. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, world opinion has become more than ever before an extremely important factor in the relationship of states, to which no state, no matter how powerful, can afford now to be indifferent.
As you know, the formulation and expression of world opinion are the direct result of the functioning of United Nations as a world forum. The interest and the solicitude of states to what is happening in other parts of the world, replacing the indifference and the isolationism of other generations, are also a direct result of the remarkable but unfortunately largely unpublicized achievements of the United Nations in the economic, social, humanitarian and cultural fields, which are certainly the true, solid infrastructure, not only of the United Nations, but of world peace as well.
I cannot help but feel, Mr. Speaker, that the Hungarian tragedy, as witnessed and judged by the United Nations, has eloquently revealed the shocking dangers of the United Nations' fundamental weakness. It has brought into clear and proper focus the fact that if the United Nations is to continue to survive, then it shall have to take the necessary steps and the necessary measures to avoid a repetition of acts which are not only contrary to the charter of the United Nations but are contrary to the elementary and basic principles

The Address-Mr. Cardin of humanity and justice. More than ever before the world looks toward the United Nations to solve efficiently international conflicts, and it expresses very bitter disappointment and disapproval whenever the United Nations fails to act quickly and promptly; and yet the very people who deplore the weaknesses of the United Nations are the very ones who are the most hesitant to give to the United Nations the power and the authority it requires to act decisively.
At the present time the United Nations is in an intolerable position. It will have to move either forward or backward. If it moves backward and the United Nations collapses, then to my mind it is world suicide. If it moves forward and acquires the necessary authority and power to act decisively, then it entails a loss of some part of our conception of national sovereignty. The question that the peoples of the world have to answer even at this time is what price they are willing to pay for world peace, and for the maximum amount of international justice and security for all nations, large and small.
I do not propose at this time, Mr. Speaker, to go into any details of the current international situation. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), in the emergency session, made a complete report on that situation and yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I believe, brought the house up to date on developments since that time; but I should like to say a few words on the Department of External Affairs. In order not to be accused of grossly lacking in modesty, may I remind hon. members that a parliamentary assistant is not a bona fide member of the department to which he is attached. I cannot therefore claim any credit for the excellent work that is now being done by the department.
During the past year I have had the privilege of attending several international gatherings and I feel quite convinced that very few Canadians indeed realize the esteem in which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Department of External Affairs are held abroad, nor do Canadians generally realize the extent to which nations from all parts of the world look to Canada for guidance and support in international affairs. Surely this fact can be interpreted as a very nice compliment to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to his department, but from this fact we must also infer a great and growing responsibility for Canada.
The Department of External Affairs, as you know, is a relatively young one and it is now in the throes of rapid expansion. The

demands that have been made for foreign service officers to fill necessary posts abroad, for the several truce commissions where Canadian participation could not be refused and more particularly to fill the ranks of the numerous divisions in the department, are so great that there is a danger the department may become understaffed. In spite of the fact that efforts have been made to encourage young men to enter the department, it has been extremely difficult if not impossible to get them in sufficient numbers and of sufficient quality to maintain the high standards of representation for which Canada is noted.
Fortunately it is not too difficult to find the reason for the present shortage of qualified candidates. To my mind the remuneration being offered is not commensurate with the training, the capacity and even the sacrifices that are demanded of a foreign service officer. Without labouring the point, I would suggest that if the government wishes to maintain its high standard of foreign service officers first of all by retaining the service officers they now have in the department and by acquiring additional qualified candidates, then I believe the government shall have to bring the remuneration now being offered into line with what is being paid to people of equal capacity and equal training working in other fields of our economy.
One of the first problems I encountered upon entering the department was a very abnormal delay in the translation of important speeches and documents arising in the department. On making inquiry it was found that the translation staff in the department was severely undermanned. Since then the Secretary of State has authorized additional translators for the department but as yet it has been impossible to find additional translators. Not because there are no translators available in Canada but rather because the remuneration that is being offered is not sufficient to encourage persons to apply for the position. What is true in the Department of External Affairs may be equally true in other fields and in other departments, and I would suggest that an inquiry into this field might be useful and timely if we wish to maintain the high standard of personnel we now have in government services.
Mr. Speaker, there is one last subject upon which I would like to say a few words. Just recently the preliminary report of the Gordon commission was published. This, of course, is a study of the numerous suggestions made over the years as to which way the government might go in order to achieve

Canada's lull economic potential. In conjunction with this report I should like to make a few very general remarks which could be interpreted as being a different aspect of the same thing.
It appears to me somehow that although Canadians generally realize that the economic, social and political changes which are taking place in the world today have a direct and important bearing upon our economy they sometimes act individually as though Canada were a self-sufficient island completely independent and secure from world economic trends. They seem to think also that although foreign economic policy may be an interesting academic exercise it really cannot affect our economic potential as guaranteed by our incalculable natural resources. I am afraid the bitter truth is that if Canadians generally do not have the moral strength or the moral courage to adapt our economy to world economic trends and if we are not prepared to face present and future economic problems in an energetic, imaginative and selfless effort to solve them, then we are not going to achieve the economic potential on which we are counting so much even now.
I presume I shall be accused in many quarters of being a pessimist, but this again is relatively unimportant if sufficient public attention can be paid to the warning signs that are now beginning to appear on our economic front. Among some of those warning signs I think we should certainly count the increasing foreign competition which is already beginning to be felt in our country, particularly from West Germany and Japan. I think it would be most unwise indeed not to envisage greater competition from a greater number of countries abroad in the future.
As we all know, the imposition of higher tariffs to protect particular industry and prices is not the answer to the problem of competition simply because we are not a self-sufficient country and must count on imports and exports as an integral part of our economy. As we know, the imposition of higher tariffs in Canada would result immediately in the imposition of higher tariffs by other countries and the subsequent decrease in our exports would seriously affect our national economy.
The solution of this problem has to be sought elsewhere and it seems to me that in accepting the advantages of a free enterprise system one must also be ready to accept the responsibilities that go with it. The problem of competition facing particular industries should be seen, studied and solved by the industries themselves as part of that responsibility. Industry in Canada has grown to its present importance by standing on its
The Address-Mr. Cardin own two feet and solving its own problems. To my mind that is not only the best, but it is the only way of solving these problems if we are to continue enjoying the free enterprise system in Canada.
Another aspect of the problem of our expanding economy is the difficulty in maintaining a balance between our increasing national production and our population. In certain quarters of this country immigration is looked upon as a source of dislocation of personnel if not of unemployment in Canada. However I feel sure that Canadians generally have the moral strength and conviction to understand and to endure the local and temporary discomforts created by immigration simply because our expanding economy demands a greater labour force and a greater home market.
Inflation is another economic problem that must be faced squarely by the Canadian public, as Mr. Muir has pointed out in the report of the Royal Bank of Canada. Methods of controlling inflation such as increasing the interest rate of bank loans, restriction of credit and any other methods of maintaining a healthy balance between available goods and the Canadian purchasing power are bound to be unpopular and give rise to a great deal of criticism and complaint. Yet everyone knows that without these economic disciplinary measures our promising Canadian future can very well be seriously jeopardized.
In the present economic situation, where there is a strong tendency toward inflation and where there is at the same time a large budgetary surplus, I feel that the best way of continuing to combat inflation and of continuing to help the general economy of the country is by engaging in the construction of essential national projects such as the St. Lawrence seaway. While I am on this subject, I should very much like to congratulate the government, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier and the St. Lawrence seaway authority on the very efficient manner in which they are carrying out what is certainly one of the greatest projects in the world.
As an important corollary to the St. Lawrence seaway, I would suggest that the project proposed by my predecessor in 1937, authorized and even started by the government, and subsequently postponed because of the second world war, be now continued. As hon. members will recall, this project called for the building of a seaway from the St. Lawrence river at Sorel along the Richelieu river to lake Champlain and across lake Champlain and down the Hudson river to New York. The United States would, of course, look after the American side of the particular project. I do not believe I need insist very much on the importance of this
232	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Cardin seaway, and although I am merely mentioning the project at this time I should like to give fair warning that I at least will do all I can to see the project put into effect as soon as possible because I believe sincerely that not only is it justified but to my mind it is an essential economic development for Canada as well as for the Richelieu river area.
Mr. Speaker, as you can see I am not really a pessimist. On the contrary, I have the greatest hopes for Canada's future. However, I do feel that if we are to reach our objective all Canadians, individually and collectively, will have to face and assume their respective responsibilities. Among these responsibilities there is one which is fundamental and yet which is sometimes ignored. It is this, that no particular interest of any one particular group of our economic life can justify endangering the common good.
As an example of what I mean, may I say that in settling the recent C.P.R. strike the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was the true champion of the common good, but I firmly believe that the fundamental responsibility was not the Prime Minister's. The common good in that particular instance was the direct responsibility of the C.P.R. and the firemen's union. They should have been able to solve their problem and come to some settlement by themselves on the strength of the responsibility that they both have to the Canadian people.
Perhaps I can make my point a little more forcibly by reminding hon. members that the persistent danger of communism is an economic one arising from ideologies which are the antithesis of our democratic form of life and our free enterprise system. If communism does not soon crumble, as we all hope it will, then sooner or later we shall have to compete economically with a form of government which recognizes no rights of individuals or groups of individuals but which channels all the energy, all the labour, all the genius, all the wealth to the exclusive use of a state which is not responsible to the people of that state. We shall also have to compete equally with state monopolies which are geared to the highest capacity of production and in which the only labour code that exists is maximum working hours for the least possible pay.
I think it would be a disastrous mistake to underestimate the dangers of an economic war with communism under those conditions. It may not be very pleasant but I think that perhaps it might be a very useful exercise to reflect seriously on these considerations in order to stop what I am afraid is a growing tendency toward materialism and toward self-centredness in the different fields


of our economic, social and political life. God has been extremely generous to Canada. He has given Canada everything we possibly need to make our country a strong, prosperous and happy country in which to live. But what we do with these God-given gifts is to my mind the direct and personal responsibility of each Canadian and each group of Canadians as well as that of the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are discussing the address in reply to the speeech from the throne and the amendment moved thereto by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the light of the fact that we are approaching a general election in the Dominion of Canada, and everything that has been said in the course of the debate so far has been, I think it is fair to say, said in the light of that fact. We were reminded of the fact that an election is imminent in the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself in which he replied to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and in which the right hon. gentleman left no doubt that an election would shortly be upon us. We were reminded of it by, amongst other speakers, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) in what I think I may fairly call a rather ungenerous and certainly very over-optimistic speech in which he made certain forecasts as to the results of that election, particularly in western Canada.
I do not wish to criticize the hon. member for being optimistic with respect to the fortunes of his own party but I think it is necessary to say that his forecasts will not be realized. It was significant that, in making his forecasts of success, he confined his attention exclusively to western Canada. I suppose that the reason is obvious in that to date his party has had some limited success in the provincial sphere in that part of the country, but the fact was very conspicuous that he did not make any forecast east of the great lakes. The hon. gentleman based his forecasts on the statement, as he put it, that his party was a party of principle.
I base my forecast of the lack of success of the Social Credit party on the fact that the people of Canada will realize that the situation that led to the success of that party in the provincial field is not duplicated in any sense in the national field. I also base it on the fact that Social Credit principles most certainly are not being applied by the provincial governments which bear that name. Inasmuch as the hon. gentleman has made it clear that the appeal of the party nationally

will be on the basis of Social Credit principles, I forecast that the appeal will be rejected because the people of Canada are not interested in Social Credit principles as enunciated by Social Credit spokesmen.
I make my forecast also on the basis that the Conservative party is a party founded on principles which established this nation, which are valid today and which are being restated and given fresh meaning under the dynamic leadership of the new Leader of the Opposition who is himself a western Canadian who knows and understands the true application of those principles to western Canada as well as to the whole of the nation. Under that leadership, with that dynamic reassertion of Conservative principles, the people of Canada will respond from west to east and will turn in increasing numbers to the Conservative party, rejecting the principles which the Social Credit party put forward.
I base my approach, however, to the fact of an election much more on the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) than on that of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). It is with respect to government policies and actions that we have phrased the motion of non-confidence that was moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) on January 9. It is with some aspects of that motion of non-confidence and the contrasting position of the two parties-I refer to the government party and the Conservative party-that I wish to deal today.
The motion of non-confidence reads as follows:
We respectfully represent that Your Excellency's advisers, by reason of their indifference, inertia and lack of leadership in the face of serious national and international problems and their disregard of the rights of parliament, are not entitled to the confidence of this house, and have lost the confidence of the people of Canada.
There are two particular things I want to mention as being issues in an election and as being facts which this house and this country will never lose sight of. The first is the conduct of the government over the years, culminating in its actions during the pipeline debate last year, when not only the supremacy of parliament but the very continuance of parliament itself as an effective instrument in our democratic process, and the very principle of responsible parliamentary government, were threatened with extinction.
The second thing that the house and the country will never forget-and should never forget-is the unsatisfactory record and attitude of this government over the years with respect to the British commonwealth of nations, culminating in the casting of a vote in the United Nations General Assembly lsftt 82715-16
The Address-Mr. Fulton November on the side of the United States and Soviet Russia and against our oldest friends, France and the United Kingdom.
The attitude of the government is also mirrored in the words of the Prime Minister on November 26 when he described the government of the United Kingdom as amongst the "supermen of Europe" and when by his words, he placed that government and the government of France in the same category as that of the communist aggressors.
Mr. Speaker, not all the honeyed words used by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) yesterday, in an obvious attempt to restore the situation and to persuade the people of Canada to forget that attitude on the part of the government, can ever remove the impression created with respect to the attitude of this government or remove from the minds of the Canadian people proof of where this government stands with respect to the British commonwealth of nations.
On the first point-with respect to the conduct and attitude of this government towards the supremacy of parliament and responsible parliamentary government-not much more needs to be done than merely to remind ourselves of the facts and the issues involved. Over the years we have seen a constant process of attack by erosion on the principles of the supremacy of parliament. It is not the supermen of Europe in this field that should concern us but rather the would-be supermen of Canada who would supplant responsible parliamentary government by cabinet dictatorship.
We saw the process brought to a peak in the defence production bill of 1955 when the rule and dictatorship of one man would have been substituted for parliamentary government. That attempt was not successful but it was carried forward and culminated in the conduct of the government during the pipe-line debate of 1956 where, for the first time in the history of a free parliament under our system, we saw an attempt to throttle debate before debate had even begun. We saw an attack on the principle of responsible parliamentary government to which the members of the government will pay lip service. They will tell the people of Canada, "Of course we believe in the principle of the supremacy of parliament and responsible parliamentary government." But the people of Canada realize that you can have responsible parliamentary government-that is that a government can be held responsible by and to parliament-only when parliament has the opportunity to examine and to discuss the government's proposals

The Address-Mr. Fulton and actions. Here we saw a deliberate move, supported by the Liberal majority and the Social Credit party in this house-and supported by the Social Credit unanimously on every occasion but one-to prevent parliament from discharging its function and duty of examining the government's proposals.

Today we see the same attitude reflected in the words of the Prime Minister, namely the attitude that discussion counts for nothing, that parliament has no right to discuss because, after all, all that matters is the will of the majority, a majority subservient to the government and doing exactly what the government tells it to do.
The government's position is that the merits of an issue are irrelevant, immaterial and should not be discussed. Everything will be decided by the vote. Why bother to discuss it? Let us have the vote now: that is exactly what the government said last session and it is what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said the other day. After the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had in a masterful speech exposed some of the issues before this house, issues which will be before the people of the country, what was the Prime Minister's answer? He said, oh, you may criticize but that does not matter because shortly we shall go through the process of "counting noses" and then all the issues will be decided.
The constitution, the rules of parliament, precedents, unwritten laws and even written laws, the merits of the situation count for nothing, and the only thing that counts in the minds of this government is the noses of the majority.

You see, Mr. Speaker, it is by remarks such as that that it is made so clear that the government, and especially the

Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), do not have the faintest understanding of the essence of parliamentary government. Of course we do not say the minority should decide, but we do say the minority has rights. We say the minority has the right of discussion. The minister and the government say there is no right of discussion; all that matters is the number of noses that are going to be evident on the side of the government. Of course, one can understand how they would arrive at that line of action because you see over there supporting them, unfortunately, so many members who are content to be deprived of the right of discussion and who are content apparently to abide by whatever the government says should be done.
The moment the government has said what it wants, they say: let us have a vote. We hear the chant: "question, question. Let us have a vote. There is no right of discussion. Discussion is irrelevant and unimportant, because if the government says it should be so, then of course it should be so and we are content to vote without discussion." All that matters, therefore, is the process of counting noses.
That process has been carried on and the rights of parliament denied and overridden to such an extent, Mr. Speaker, that we have now very nearly reached the point of no return beyond which it will be difficult indeed, if not impossible, to restore the principle of the supremacy of parliament and of responsible parliamentary government. The people of Canada here face a very serious issue, a domestic crisis every bit as important as the international crises which have occupied so much of our attention. There is only one solution to that crisis and that is to remove from office a government which denies the supremacy of parliament, is not willing to accept the principle of responsible parliamentary government, and to replace it by a government which is dedicated to the preservation of this principle as the Conservative party and its leader are dedicated.
The second issue which is before the country is the attitude of this government with regard to the British commonwealth. It was interesting to observe yesterday, on what I might almost call commonwealth day, the attempts by government spokesmen to remove the unfortunate, indeed the disastrous, impressions created by their conduct and their words last November. We see a picture of a government desperately trying to make amends; a government as aware as we are that an election is facing them shortly, and trying to remove that impression. It is no wonder they do so because they know all tile damage that their conduct and their words

have done to their support in the country. We saw the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) praise the commonwealth, praise the United Kingdom and tell the house how there may have been temporary differences of opinion but these really only strengthened the bond; how they knew all along the government of the United Kingdom, however its individual actions may be judged, is nevertheless dedicated to peace.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), after he had finished his travelogue, was at pains to impress upon the house how everywhere he went in Asia, with every government representative with whom he had discussions and in the villages where he went, he was at pains to impress upon the people the dedication of the United Kingdom government to peace, and the progress that had been made under the aegis of the government of that country.
Unfortunately, from the government's point of view, from Canada's point of view and the world's point of view, you cannot turn on the stream of unity and co-operation and then turn if off again like a tap. The stream is based on continuous understanding, continuous sympathy and the continued maintenance of mutual interests and must be kept flowing or it will dry up. It cannot be turned off and on again like a tap.
This government cannot thus easily repair the damage done by their actions and by the Prime Minister's words last year when he lumped together the governments of the United Kingdom and France in the same category of aggressors as the communist governments of Russia and the other socialist soviet republics. Remember the Prime Minister's words in that regard on November 26. Having referred to the governments of the United Kingdom and France, he went on to say, as recorded at page 20 of Hansard for that date:
I have been scandalized more than once by the attitude of the larger powers, the big powers as we call them, who have all too frequently treated the charter of the United Nations as an instrument with which to regiment smaller nations-
Including in those words the governments of the United Kingdom and of France,-

-one of them a government which the Secretary of State for External Affairs was at pains yesterday to point out had built for itself a glorious tradition- that is what he called it-of bringing to a state of independence, self-government and autonomy, nations which have never known that condition before. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to observe that in all of the reasons given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the Minister of National Health and Welfare yesterday, as to the things which now mean so much to Canada in the commonwealth and the things which should unite us in the commonwealth, it was interesting that in all this panegyric which they sang yesterday, there was not one mention of that factor which we always understood to be at the centre of commonwealth unity, and that is, loyalty to the crown. There was no mention in either of those speeches yesterday of the principle of loyalty to the crown, to the monarchy which, as I understand it, is the central theme and uniting factor of the commonwealth.
The government's action against the United Kingdom and France was previously justified on the basis that there was danger in the Suez situation of the commonwealth splitting; that it could not stand the pressures created by the action then taken. Later on that was denied by Mr. Casey in Australia. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) then modified his statement as to what he had meant. He said that he had referred exclusively to the Asian members of the commonwealth. Well, now, unfortunately, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has shown himself to be prone to rather loose terminology in this connection. It will be recalled that at one stage, after the fighting had begun, he said, referring to the commonwealth, that it was on the verge of dissolution and he further said that "was not an exaggerated observation". He is guilty of several contradictions in this matter.
Since that time, after being contradicted himself by the Australian spokesman, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said he was referring exclusively to the Asian members of the commonwealth. Shortly thereafter the prime minister of Ceylon, who was interviewed at the United Nations where he was while all these discussions were going on, said, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of December 3, that he thought Mr. Pearson's commons statement was "rather an exaggeration".
Then it will be recalled that yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs repeated in this house the same thing, namely, that the separatist pressures were tremendous and that he felt it had been quite possible that the commonwealth might split up. He was asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) whether that had not been denied by the governments of

The Address-Mr. Fulton Ceylon and India and he replied that it had been denied by the prime minister of Ceylon, but that he had been informed by the very highest authority in the government of India that there had been danger of India leaving the commonwealth. Well, sir, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is contradicted there by no less a person than the prime minister of India himself who, speaking in Ottawa, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of December 24, said-and the reporter, Mr. Hume, says that these are Mr. Nehru's own words:
India wishes, quite clearly, to have her commonwealth association continued; there are so many disruptive tendencies in the world that I am not prepared to break up any kind of association or bridge that there is. I never thought India's commonwealth association should be broken, despite grave differences of opinion.
He went on to say that some important people in India suggested the commonwealth association was doing no good. He continued:
We discussed the question in our congress recently and we are firmly of the opinion that we wish our association with the commonwealth to continue. In spite of differences within the commonwealth, we felt that it is a helpful association in the larger causes of peace in the world.
Now, there is the prime minister of India speaking and saying that he never thought they should get out of the commonwealth. And yet, the Secretary of State for External Affairs only yesterday told us that he was informed by the highest authority in the government of India that they had been in danger of withdrawing. What have we? Have we a completely inaccurate statement, or does the Secretary of State for External Affairs suggest that there is a higher authority than the prime minister? Can it possibly be, Mr. Speaker, that the eulogy given to him by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. LaUrent) in this house the other day has already gone to his head? Does he think there are higher authorities in government than the prime minister? For that is the only inference we can draw from his statement, unless we are to believe that notwithstanding having been corrected, he still persists in a deliberate inaccuracy and misrepresentation.
Other unfortunate effects which flowed from the government's action last November, and which are now obvious to the Canadian people, in addition to the damage that it did to the principle of commonwealth solidarity, have been, of course, to place Canada in a position where she must accept dictation from Nasser in Egypt. This the government still persists in denying in spite of the most obvious facts which prove it, such as that Canada's original intention as to the type of troops she should send was not allowed to be

fulfilled, and also by the comments made by authoritative sources elsewhere. I have here the New York Sunday Times of January 13, which contains an article by Thomas J. Hamilton. The article is headed:
United Nations Suez Intervention Restores Status Quo
Nasser Is Still In Full Control Of The Canal With His Future Terms For Operation Unchanged
The correspondent is reporting on the discussion at the United Nations and says as follows:
But the friends of Britain, France and Israel insist that practically every decision has been in accord with Egyptian demands.
He is referring to the decision with regard to the clearing of the canal and the role of United Nations emergency force. He continues:
This, they say, is illustrated both by the handling of the United Nations emergency force and the salvage operation. Egypt, despite denials, is exerting her veto on the countries participating in the emergency force, as witness the fact that Canada, which sponsored the idea, has been allowed to contribute only non-combat troops.
As Egypt demanded, the force has been withdrawn from the Suez canal zone, permitting the complete establishment of Egyptian control. Egyptian troops are advancing into the Sinai peninsula behind the United Nations force, and will soon re-establish Colonel Nasser's control there, leaving the United Nations force to act only as a buffer between the Egyptian and Israeli troops.
According to a spokesman for Mr. Hammarskjold, the general assembly, not Egypt, will decide when the United Nations force is to be withdrawn. But Mr. Hammarskj old's insistence upon respecting the "sovereign rights" of Egypt increases the probability that the assembly will tell the force to leave whenever Egypt says so.
So it is undeniable, Mr. Speaker, if one faces facts, that the result of the government's action has been to place Canada, along with other countries, in the position of having to accept the dictation of Egypt, thus making it very unlikely that there will be a satisfactory over-all settlement of the dispute which gave rise to this whole situation.
That, then, is the damage that has been done,-damage to the commonwealth, damage to the possibility of an over-all satisfactory solution to the Middle East question-done by the unfortunate acts of this government. But the damage has been done; and although it is essential that we understand the basis upon which we now rest, it is still more important to look forward and to discuss ways and means of repairing that damage. This is going to involve work, not more pious platitudes such as we heard yesterday from the two government spokesmen who were concerned not so much to tell us what they were going to do, as to try to pretend that no damage had been caused by the government's unfortunate action.

To repair the damage is going to require work. Why should we not have the Quebec conference that was suggested by the Leader of the Opposition last November? The Prime Minister has not given a single reason why it should not be held. He dismissed it with another series of generalities. Unfortunately, we have not heard from the government any positive proposals in this respect. We are back where we have been for many years because, of course, our quarrel with the government with regard to its attitude to the commonwealth does not stem only from the time of the Suez crisis; it antedates it by many years.
Our quarrel with the government is that they have done nothing for years beyond paying lip service to the idea of the commonwealth. They have indulged in vague generalities, they have made no positive contribution and they have made no earnest or consistent attempt to institute a series of commonwealth discussions which would be designed to arrive at common objectives and a common understanding and common approaches to these world problems, and especially to arrive at these common approaches before the problems reach disaster proportions. It is no wonder therefore that the Suez explosion caught us all unawares.
There had been a conference not very long before that, the last commonwealth prime ministers' conference. You will remember the strenuous effort we on this side made, first of all to get the Prime Minister at least to see to it that there was an agenda and that Canada was going over there prepared to engage in serious discussions in regard to the matters that would come before the conference, but this was not done. No such thing occurred to the Prime Minister's mind. He was going over there for a nice trip. That was at the time when Cyprus was in danger of becoming an explosive area; it was at a time when the whole Middle Eastern situation was brewing.
The Prime Minister returned from the conference and you will remember how strenuously we pressed him to give us a report concerning what was discussed and what was decided. We were interested in knowing if anything at all had been said about Cyprus or about the Middle East. No. He reported he had lunch with Mr. Nehru and they had a pleasant time at the conference. They had issued a nice communique and there had been a feeling of good will and good relations had been established. That is all we got out of the Prime Minister because that is all the Prime Minister went over there to do.
We have pointed out for years that no international association will mean anything
The Address-Mr. Fulton nor can it mean anything unless the members of the association and particularly the senior members such as Canada intend that it'i should mean something and intend to make it work. This business of saying the commonwealth is a force for world peace and that Canada's position in foreign affairs and in international relationships is influenced in large measure by the fact that she is a member of the commonwealth and her membership in the commonwealth is something desirable to maintain, is simply to voice meaningless platitudes unless the government does something, first to decide what it is the commonwealth should mean in world affairs and in our own national interest, and then does some work to make it realize those things.
In our view the preservation of the commonwealth is a matter of interest to all of Canada and not just something to which we have a sentimental attachment. It is a matter of vital national concern to all parts of Canada and to all peoples in Canada to an equal degree because it is based upon and has at its centre the monarch, the crown. This is the very centre and core of our national existence and our form of government as a constitutional and monarchial democracy. It is essential to us also because as a member of the commonwealth we can have a wider influence in international affairs, a fuller being if you like, than we would ever have as a separate nation.
It is important to us, Mr. Speaker, also because it is more than ever essential that there should be a strong and united commonwealth as a factor in the preservation of world peace. I was not at all satisfied and I am sure many hon. members were not fully satisfied, indeed they must have been deeply disturbed, by the readiness yesterday of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to write off the commonwealth as a factor in the preservation of world peace, when he Said in effect there is only one country in the western world in a position to discharge truly worldwide responsibilities today, the United States. Sir, we believe that the commonwealth, if recreated and built into that force which it could and should be, is also in a position to discharge worldwide responsibilities and is also in a position to exercise worldwide influence. As Mr. Menzies of Australia said when discussing the last commonwealth prime ministers' conference and his dissatisfaction with what had been done and particularly his dissatisfaction with the communique that had been issued, "A state- '-rhent' of that kind should and could carry the moral authority * that the commonwealth

The Address-Mr. Fulton should possess. I think the world needs the force of judgment that the commonwealth has."
We are in complete agreement with those words. The commonwealth will not possess that moral authority and certainly will not possess that physical authority unless some work is done to recreate it and to give to it the meaning which it should have. This certainly will not be accomplished by the words and attitudes of the Prime Minister of last November and the actions of the government at that time. It certainly will not be achieved by the inaction and pious platitudes which is all we can get from the government today.
We are therefore left with certain questions which emerge from this whole situation. First, what is the government's policy with regard to the United Nations emergency force? We were told yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he believed we should work toward the creation of a permanent United Nations force; but the country was told by the other secretary of state for external affairs who is presently officially the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that it is impractical to have a permanent United Nations force. He did admit to an honest difference of opinion with the Prime Minister on that score but we did not realize that, having just returned from this tour he undertook, he would so deliberately and definitely state a view contrary to that expressed officially on behalf of the government in the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Who is the Secretary of State for External Affairs? What is the policy of the government?

Surely the people of Canada are entitled to know that and the people of Canada are particularly entitled to know what is the policy of this government with respect to Canada's component in the present United Nations emergency force in Egypt. Is it to be just what Nasser says? Is it to be withdrawn just when Nasser says it is to be withdrawn? Is it to do only that which Nasser says it is to do? What does the government of Canada feel about that? And if they reply that these things should be decided by the United Nations, what recommendations are they going to make to the United Nations on the basis of which a decision will be taken? Are we to accept the fact that not only the Canadian government but the United Nations general assembly with the consent of the Canadian government is to have its decisions made by the dictator of Egypt?
The next question, and it is really the larger question, is this. What does this

government propose to do to restore and maintain commonwealth unity? Yesterday we heard the words of the government ministers telling us what importance they attach to the recreation of commonwealth unity but we heard nothing except words. We have heard nothing but words for years; we have seen no action. We made a concrete suggestion in November with a view to the restoration of both commonwealth unity and the Atlantic alliance-the holding of a conference in Quebec. That was only one suggestion, but even that suggestion has been rejected, and nothing, absolutely nothing, has been offered in its stead.
Mr. Speaker, we are left in the position that, with respect to this whole question of the most vital and fundamental of Canada's interests in world affairs, the government has nothing to offer. Its actions and the words of its Prime Minister have been a disaster and have weakened our position. On this issue, as on the issue of parliamentary supremacy, I have no doubt what will be the verdict of the Canadian people in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I wish at the outset to extend my warmest congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robi-chaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I congratulate them particularly for having spoken with such eloquence a tongue which is not their mother tongue. We have there an example of good understanding and of bilingualism which should be appreciated and practiced more often.
I wish also to extend my congratulations to the new Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the high position which has been bestowed upon him after so many efforts on his part and in spite of the little support he got from the delegates of my province. It is not every party leader who can get a unanimous vote on a first try, it is not everybody who can be elected by acclamation. Be that as it may, I extend to him my most sincere wishes and I hope he may remain for a long time the leader of his party and the Leader of the Opposition.
I would like now, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words on the social security legislation which the Canadian people enjoy thanks to the initiative and the concern of the Liberal

government, and more particularly on the subject of old age pensions. Canadians everywhere have asked that the old age pension now enjoyed by people 70 years old and over be increased by $10 to $20.
We must realize that this old age security legislation has not been enacted to take care of all the needs of the recipient, but rather to help and assist our older citizens in general. However there is nothing to prevent our provincial government, as it is done in other provinces, from adding $10 or $20 to the $40 now granted by the federal government.
It is clear that we must do all we can to help those unfortunates who, having toiled all their lives, find themselves without any means of support.
I realize, as do all hon. members, that this amount of $40 is not sufficient and that, were it possible to increase it, it would provide our older people with greater comfort and security. On the other hand, though I am not opposed to this increase, I do think that it would be preferable to extend the scope of the legislation by extending its benefits to a greater number of old people.
I have often noticed in my constituency, that many people aged 60 and over who, for reasons of health or physical disability, are obliged to quit work, of their own volition or at the request of their employers, are, in most cases, in a very poor financial situation, they have difficulty in meeting their vital obligations during the period extending between 60 and 65, with regard to which our social security legislation provides no security at all. Briefly, this is the plan I suggest. At the present time, the federal government is, without a means test, paying the full amount of the old age pension from the age of 70 on. From 65 to 70, the pension is paid to those who can meet the means test, half the required sum being provided by the federal government and the other half by the provinces concerned. I suggest that those old age pensions entirely provided by the federal government be paid from the age of 65 years on, while pensions paid to the poor old people by the federal government and the provinces be paid when these people reach the age of 60. By extending in this way the scope of the legislation, instead of by increasing the pension, we would be doing service to a larger number of people. In other words, by lowering the
The Address-Mr. Fontaine age of eligibility by five years the present legislation would be made more efficient than would be the case were the amount of pension merely increased, an increase which by the way could be met by the provinces.
With regard to family allowances, I am of the opinion that the time has come for the government to make a serious study of the possibility of increasing them. This increase, a necessary one, would be such as to improve the standard of living of Canadian families and more particularly of larger families. As was pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) the cost of living has gone up tremendously over the past ten years, but the needs have not diminished. We should increase the means of providing for the needs of our children in proportion to the increased expense involved. For my part, I suggest that these allowances be increased in proportion to the increase in the cost of living, that is for example by paying $6, $9 and $12.
From the field of social security I now pass to that of agriculture. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of representing a constituency which has been particularly blessed by Providence, because of the fact that it is situated in the richest area of the province of Quebec, an area which is well suited to all types of farming and which is called the Richelieu valley.
By far the greatest number of farmers of my constituency carry out specialized farming, more particularly sugar beet production which, in the course of the last year, has brought in a revenue of over half a million dollars in my district. They have also carried on tomato-growing on a large scale, the produce being shipped to metropolitan markets as well as to rural canning plants.
May I be allowed by the way to congratulate the co-operative canneries on the excellence of their organization which has greatly contributed to the improvement of the lot of our farmers. In this regard, I would feel remiss in my duty were I not to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) most sincerely for the precious aid which he has provided the poultry farmers of my district. A poultry experimental station constructed at St. Damase in 1945 has just undergone considerable changes. The extension of the building and the construction of immense refrigerating rooms allow that co-operative to improve its commercial position, not only on the local market but also on the inter-
240	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fontaine national market. The poultry co-operative of St. Damase is considered by experts to be one of the largest and most modern in the country. That achievement was made possible by the co-operation of the federal Department of Agriculture. Besides being a monument to the credit of our agricultural class, it will contribute greatly to the constant improvement of the agricultural economy of our area.
Before passing on to another subject, I should like to say a few words on butter. The price support given us by the federal government for a number of years was highly advantageous to us of the dairy industry.
Having always considered agriculture as the basis of a successful economy, the federal government took the initiative of authorizing the Minister of Agriculture to help our agricultural class by means of grants and price support enactments, being convinced that such legislation would primarily promote the interests of the country at large.
Indeed, experience has shown us that when agriculture is prosperous in a country, all classes of society benefit from it. The dairy industry in general and, in particular, the milk producers shipping their milk to creameries and cheese factories were saved from bankruptcy by the act on the support of the price of butter. That act is unquestionably the one that rendered the greatest service to our agricultural class and particularly, I might add, to the farmers of my province, because the dairy industry remains the main source of income of the Quebec farmers.
According to our legislation, Canadian farmers can benefit from the act until its expiration in May, 1958. I urge the Minister of Agriculture to extend the duration of this act for an indefinite period, because I dare say our dairy industry was saved by the price support enactment and it is most important that it be maintained in force. I would even say that this act protects not only the producer but also the consumer. It has the dual effect of preventing the exaggerated speculation that was carried on in connection with our dairy products. It is not surprising that the speculators should have focussed their attention on butter in particular. Everybody remembers that, before the enactment of that measure, producers during the season of plenty, were paid ridiculous prices for their products which brought them no profit and, most of the time, left them with a deficit. On the other hand, in winter time


when production slows down, the price of butter was going up every day and the consumers had to pay excessive prices for that product. Speculators were thus in a position to gain unlimited profits on a product which, after all, brought no profit at all to the producers in most cases.
Mr. Speaker, this problem has been solved by our act on the support of butter prices and it is very important, in fact essential, that our farmers should never again have to put up with situations such as that.
The need for this beneficial measure continues to be felt; therefore, I can only wish, -I know beforehand that this wish will be met,-that the government will go on with that policy which has been so profitable and which is more and more appreciated by our farmers.
Mr. Speaker, another subject dealing with agriculture and also of a vital importance for our specialized farmers is the question of the great metropolitan market of Montreal. This matter concerns more particularly the producers specialized in horticulture who live around the city of Montreal. The development of the metropolitan market is at present underway. Construction was begun last spring and this project will soon be completed if all the authorities concerned give their support and the necessary financial assistance to those in charge of that undertaking. The city of Montreal considers this project as most important and it has already paid a generous contribution. An amount of one million dollars has also been granted by the government of my province. I wish here to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for his generous co-operation. Since this market will not be exclusively a local market but also an interprovincial market, I feel that the federal government should contribute to such an undertaking which, I repeat, is of vital importance for agriculture, and especially for the producers specialized in horticulture.
Mr. Speaker, horticulturists are the victims of undue speculation; it is essential that federal authorities should help this category of producers as they have done for the dairy farmers. Otherwise, we will be faced with the disappearance of these specialists in horticulture. I do believe that the federal authorities should act and make a substantial grant for this project, a grant at least matching the amount the province of Quebec has agreed to pay to this organization.

Mr. Speaker, as the time allotted to me does not permit my informing this house in detail of the record I have before me, and which proves that the federal authorities would be well advised in helping to carry out this plan, I shall just advance a few arguments that will justify my remarks at this time. The Montreal market is a receiving and distributing centre for the fruit and vegetable trade, not only on a local and provincial basis, but on a national and even international scale. The Montreal market is the main distribution centre for fruit and vegetables in Canada. In 1952, arrivals of these commodities on the Montreal market by rail only amounted to 18,951 carloads, coming from eight Canadian provinces, eleven foreign countries and thirty-four American states. These figures are taken from a report on arrivals of fruit and vegetables on Canadian markets, published in 1952 by the marketing division of the federal Department of Agriculture in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne mentions a proposed amendment extending the scope of the Municipal Grants Act to authorize the payment of grants in lieu of taxes on federal property in municipalities where such property benefits from municipal services. The government deserves congratulations for including this project in the speech from the throne. The grants will, in most cases, be of great help to the municipalities, and bring some relief to taxpayers. Due to the rapid expansion of house construction in Canada since the war, our municipalities have been faced with serious problems which in most cases they cannot solve without the help of the federal and provincial governments. As far as I am concerned, I am glad that this project will be submitted to the hon. members for approval during this session.
May I say just a few words about grants to universities? I will merely state that I share the view of the hon. member from Hull (Mr. Caron). An unconditional grant to all the universities is not in itself undue interference in the field of education. If foreign millionaires are allowed to make a gift to our universities and to our classical colleges, why should we not grant the same privilege to the federal government? It is sheer demagogy to hold the opposite view. Besides, our people from Quebec, just as the people of other provinces, have contributed to the consolidated revenue fund from which those amounts are drawn. Why should we not benefit from
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron
it, as others do, rather than seek to keep to ourselves, in a special reserve, for the sake of so-called autonomy? Are not the people of Quebec Canadians just like the people of the other provinces?
I am just about through with the few remarks I had planned to make. However I would not like to sit down without telling the hon. Prime Minister of the satisfaction of our people concerning the excellent administration of the affairs of his government -our government-and because of what he has himself contributed to the country since he has become our leader. But what is still more admirable is the fact that not only is our prime minister respected and admired by his opponents but the leaders of foreign countries look upon him as a first-rate statesman, one worthy of their confidence.
It is not my business to discuss foreign affairs, but since the world seems to be unanimous about the excellent part played by Canada in the United Nations and in NATO through our minister for external affairs (Mr. Pearson), I can only join the members who spoke before me, to offer him sincere and well deserved compliments and to wish that Providence will long preserve men of such value.
If I had the time, I could analyse the moral and economic condition in which people of other countries are living-and I could even say people of all countries-and I am convinced, in the present situation, that there could be, in any case, only one conclusion, which is that today, in 1957, it is rewarding to be able to call ourselves Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I almost hesitate to say so but it is twenty years this year since I first sat in a legislative assembly. During those years I think it is perhaps safe to say that I have always taken somewhat of a relish in being able to heave as sharply pointed bricks as possible at the various governments opposite whom I have sat during that time. But periodically during that time the governments which I have opposed have-inadvertently, of course-done something of which I have approved; and always, when they have done that, I have found myself hesitant in attack, a still small voice, as someone said, crying "fiddlesticks". This morning, as I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), that still small voice was extremely vocal within me.

The Address-Mr. C. Cameron
This government has done in the past and undoubtedly will do in the future many things for which they merit severe criticism and attack. But in order to make our attacks effective when we make them, I think we should be careful not to attack on the wrong occasion or for the wrong thing. During the special session of parliament I did not take part in the debate because there appeared no necessity for my doing so. The government's actions were those I thought were in the interest of Canada, and I imagined that they would have plenty of people to support those actions in the house.
I listened at that time with great interest to the speeches of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). In the past I have not always agreed with the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Sometimes I think he has fallen far short of what we should expect of Canada's principal international spokesman. However, I think it is only fair to say that on that occasion I think no intelligent Canadian could really have quarrelled with what he had to tell us. He spoke obviously as a man deeply anxious over a critical and dangerous situation, not in any boastful manner, recounting the efforts of himself and his colleagues to deal with an appalling world situation. I also think it is fair to say that he expressed at that time a deep concern over the tragic cleavage that had taken place between Canada and her two oldest allies.
I think those things should be said because this morning and during the special session suggestions were made that, in the course followed by the government at that time, Canada had in some way betrayed the commonwealth that Canada had in some way scorned and affronted our oldest allies. It seems to me to be an extraordinary situation that Canadians can stand up in this parliament and suggest that, because a strain was put upon the relationship within the commonwealth-not by Canada or not by any action of Canada's-we are to blame for that strain.
I found the speech made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) this morning most interesting. As a matter of fact I felt as though it had great anthropological interest, I might even say biological interest, because it struck me that it was the same sort of interest that would have been aroused if one were to encounter on the streets of Ottawa mastodons or dinosaurs from the dim and distant past. In the course of the hon. member's remarks it became quite obvious

that in the view of the official opposition there is only one nation in the world which has the right to sovereignty and that is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that he deplored the actions of Mr. Dag Hammarskjold in insisting that the sovereign rights of Egypt should be respected. Apparently that is outrageous. Because we do not like Mr. Nasser, because we do not like some of the things he has done, because we consider-probably quite rightly-that he is a rather hardboiled dictator, we are to take the position that the sovereign rights of the country that he happens to rule can be flouted at will.
We were told this morning that the main strains were placed on the commonwealth by the action taken by the Canadian government. In the first place I think perhaps we are flattering ourselves in thinking that the Canadian government was quite such a decisive factor in the situation. In the second place, I could not help feeling this morning- as I felt on an earlier occasion during the special session-that there are members of the official opposition whose conception of the commonwealth of nations is rigidly confined to members of the nations of European stock, and that the idea that such new members as India, Pakistan and Ceylon should be consulted, that their views should be considered, is something entirely foreign to that concept.
During the special session I was interested not only to hear what the Prime Minister of Canada had to say with regard to the world situation but also in the extraordinary reactions that were aroused by his statements. His statements were repeated again or quoted this morning by the hon. member for Kamloops in an extremely deprecatory manner, as I recall it. On one occasion the Prime Minister remarked that he had often been scandalized by the actions of the great powers in the United Nations. My criticism of the Prime Minister would be that he then said something that should have been said long before, that he waited until he was exasperated to say something that should have been said earlier in measured and more magisterial terms. There is not an intelligent student of public affairs in the world today who has not been painfully conscious of that scandalous attitude and action of the great powers to which the Prime Minister referred.
He also had a remark to make with regard to the supermen of Europe. That apparently is something that should not be said, but all history supports that statement. The sooner we of the Caucasian races remember that the last 300 years carry an almost unbroken history of pillage, rapine, and bloody

suppression of all non-European people with whom we came in contact, the sooner we shall be prepared to live at peace with the human race. While we may want to forget that nasty skeleton in our cupboard or clothe it with the myth of the white man's burden, let us not make any mistake about this fact: the peoples of Asia and of Africa have not forgotten. An attitude of humility with regard to the deplorable record of our ancestors and, indeed, of some of our contemporaries of the European races would be in order today.
Again, my criticism of the Prime Minister would be that he said this in a moment of exasperation when it should have been said again and again by the spokesman of such countries of Canada, which, while inhabited by people of European stock, had itself to break loose from that control and rule by the supermen of Europe.
No, Mr. Speaker; I do not think those are things for which either the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs is to be blamed or criticized. Nor are they statements for which I think any Canadian should feel the need to apologize.
But I have noted, sir, in this present session that apparently we are beginning to move away from that rather forthright position. I think that is a tragedy because I am sure there are many Canadians, like myself, who feel that during those critical days in November of last year Canada, for the first time, emerged from the shadows and became a definite international entity with clearly defined features rather than remaining, as we had hitherto, a rather vague, shadowy figure, obscured in the mists of a sort of general amiability. I am sorry to note by the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and indeed by that of the Prime Minister also in this session, that they appear to be retreating from that firm position. I suppose it is a case of coming events casting their shadows before them.
It may be true, as the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) suggested, that government spokesmen feel there has been an antagonism to the attitude taken by this government during the world crisis last fall. Undoubtedly there has been some antagonism. I suppose that in the constituency I represent there are more people of immediately British origin than in any other part of the Dominion of Canada. There are, moreover, amongst those people probably a larger proportion of people coming from those social brackets in Britain which would normally adopt an extremely conservative and rather imperialistic point of view. It is true that amongst my constituents there are a number who would wax just as indignant as the
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron hon. member for Kamloops and his colleagues in this house. There are also a significant number of others who, like myself, feel sorry and grieved that the nation of which we are natives should have been betrayed in that particular instance, betrayed from the position of international probity which had been built up over the last decade or two.
I would suggest to the members of this government that it would be better to run the risk of losing a certain measure of support throughout the country and to maintain that solid, unequivocal attitude which was presented to us during the special session of the house. We should remember also that we should not confuse the people of Britain with a small group which, for the time being, happens to be in control of the destinies of that country. Not for nothing did two ministers of the crown resign in the face of the incalculable follies committed their government. Not for nothing did every responsible organ of public opinion in Great Britain condemn and deplore what was being done. We in Canada shall not be discharging the responsibility of friendship for the people of Britain unless we speak with an unequivocal voice in support of this element in Britain, the most intelligent, the best informed, who have deplored the train of events which took place last fall and which will have in the future incalculable results for the unfortunate people of Great Britain. I should like to see our government, as I say, maintain that solid position which it assumed during the crisis of last fall at the United Nations, and not pay attention to the possible unpopularity in certain quarters that will be coming because of that position.
I think we must be careful not to condone follies when the fool is a beloved fool; not to condone evil on the doctrine that good might have come out of evil. Good never comes out of evil. Men, women and children were killed; their lives destroyed and their homes broken. No matter what the purpose may have been, that in itself was an evil action. If we are going to assume a position in the world commensurate with our material power, then we have to be prepared to continue condemning evil, reprobating folly whoever may commit it.
I think, sir, while these events of the past have been important in two regards, one in placing Canada firmly before the world in a certain posture and the other in revealing to us the political thinking of the various sections of the Canadian community, what is more important is what is to take place in the future. I was interested yesterday to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs suggesting that we must work towards

The Address-Mr. C. Cameron a permanent United Nations force. I hope when that proposal is carried into effect that perhaps the procedure that was followed in the setting up of the emergency force may be borne in mind, because to me one of the most significant aspects of the establishment of the United Nations emergency force was that it was action on the part of the small, medium-sized nations of this world, behaving I think somewhat in the spirit of the Prime Minister's condemnation of the great powers of the world, in a spirit of impatience with these great powers who can never refrain from grinding their own axes.
I should like to see such a permanent force remain as a force contributed to by the small and medium sized powers of the world because then it could be a force that would not be embroiled in the power politics of one or the other of the larger powers in the world today. I think there is something else we can do now as a result of recent events. I think there can be no question that the appalling series of events in Hungary has struck a blow at the Soviet union that perhaps no one can as yet assess. In my opinion it has completely altered the military picture of the world because not only can the Soviet union now no longer rely on the peoples and the armed forces of satellite nations in the event of a conflict, they have been informed in unmistakable terms that these will be enemies within their gates. I think we should take advantage of that situation. It seems to me that here is a case where some hard-hearted bargaining could be done with the communist world. I cannot believe that the men in the Kremlin today are very anxious to continue to have these potential enemies ready to stab them in the back if they got involved in a war. It seems to me that the part of wisdom for them would be, and I do not think you should consider they are without wisdom, to relinquish their hold over these satellite states under an agreement whereby they become a neutral belt between the west and the east. I think that will have possibilities also of solving one of the sore spots in the world today, one of the trouble spots that may well cause great concern to the rest of the world, and that is divided Germany.
