speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to join the previous speakers in extending sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. There is no doubt, at least as far as I am concerned, that the respective electors of these hon. members will have every reason to be proud of their representatives.
The speech from the throne deals with many subjects which are all interesting. There is one however which seems to be of prime importance in the eyes of the government since nearly half of that important document has been devoted to it. I refer to the position of Canada with respect to world conditions.
Since I wish to limit my remarks to a single question, for the time being at least, I thought I would deal with a question related to that problem and which I consider very important. I mean the eventual representation of Canada at the Holy See in Rome.
Besides, for a good many years a great number of the electors I have the pleasure and the privilege of representing in this house have been good enough to let me know their views on that subject. Now it so happens that all were in favour of such representation. It is indeed a pleasure for me to lay their views before this house.
I do not think that there is one Canadian province where certain individuals, certain patriotic, religious or other groups have not expressed a similar opinion. On the other hand, I know that in those same provinces other individuals and other similar groups have expressed an opposite view. Which means of course that we have there a much debated and debatable problem whose solution is not self-evident but must be looked for in a cool and objective way, according to the best interests of the Canadian nation.
In foreign countries, Canada maintains 46 diplomatic posts filled either by an ambassador, a minister or a high commissioner, together with a great number of consuls, attaches, commercial representatives, various officers, and so on. For the year 1956-57, according to the estimates voted in this house last year, the cost of maintaining these posts, alone, including salaries, amounted to $7,210,961.
On the other hand, 46 foreign countries maintain here a similar diplomatic representation whose cost is likely just as high. These figures, reporting the number of


countries as well as the expenses, give us an idea of the importance attached by various states, Canada included, to their diplomatic representation.
Besides, especially in recent years our policy, domestic as well as foreign, is established with due regard for the international situation. It is no doubt with this in mind that the Canadian government, besides maintaining permanent diplomatic representatives, very often sends itinerant diplomats, in most cases a member of the cabinet, to some remote corner of the world. It thus once again emphasizes the importance of going abroad to gather useful information, to make known what we believe should be known and also no doubt to disguise what we want to keep to ourselves.
There are in the world posts of superior strategic value where information of vital importance is concentrated or which constitute a source of such information. Such posts are just as so many cross-roads where the diplomats of almost every country come into contact. It so happens that one of these posts is in the Vatican state of Rome. Here are some facts and figures which show the importance of this post. The Holy See sends diplomatic representatives to 41 countries among which are France, Germany, India, Italy and Spain, plus several apostolic delegates of which one is here, in Canada.
On the other hand there are in the Vatican state 45 diplomatic missions among which are to be found missions from some of the greatest countries in the world such as Great Britain, France, Germany, India and Spain. Certain countries which do not even deem it necessary to send representatives to Canada have representatives to the Holy See. And even the most powerful of all countries, the United States had personal representatives under three successive presidents, who felt this to be a most pressing need after diplomatic relations had been severed with the Vatican state.
Still Canada has not as yet thought it necessary to have its own representative in this world centre of a diplomacy of the highest standards.
I hope that no one will suggest that we cannot have a diplomatic representative there because the Pope happens to be the religious head of the church. In that case we could hardly maintain diplomatic representation in the United Kingdom where the supreme head of the nation is also the supreme head of the

established church. In any event, no impartial person has ever suggested that the Pope, even when he was unjustly dispossessed, has not always been and still is not the uncontested sovereign of a temporal state, small of course, but quite real and which has its own autonomous and sovereign government. It is precisely because this state is very small in area and because its leader has no territorial ambition whatever that the other states should feel reassured with regard to the objectivity of the information they may gather there as well as to the impartiality and independence with which would be greeted suggestions or proposals they might wish to submit. We are thus protected against certain interested manoeuvres which may have been quite common in the Middle Ages or during the Renaissance, when the popes not only had to manage the church but also had the duty, like the leaders of other states of that time, to protect and defend the temporal kingdom committed to their care.
Furthermore, if it is feared in some quarters, that if we have a representative at the Vatican, we must share the religious belief of the Holy Father, does it mean that we necessarily share the beliefs of the leaders of communist countries where we do have representatives? Why then the double standard? A narrow, inconsiderate one with regard to a sovereign who, beyond any doubt, wants peace and order in the world, and a generous and broad-minded one in dealing with the leaders of countries, which, no less surely, for they themselves say it and prove it- want trouble, discord, and misery in the world, the better to establish their barbaric domination and their godless materialism, destructive of the freedom and happiness of peoples.
Thirty-two of our 46 missions abroad are headed by ambassadors, two of them being in iron curtain countries, i.e., in the U.S.S.R. and Yugoslavia. We have also ministers in two other communist countries, Poland and Czechoslovakia. Until last year, we maintained for years an embassy in the Argentine, while the president of that country was trying hard, and sometimes by ignoble means, to foil the legitimate religious or national aspirations of the Argentine people.
To follow through a comparison between the leaders of those countries I just mentioned and the admirable man who is now presiding over the destinies of Vatican City, would be an insult to the intelligence of honourable members, and I do not want to press it any further.
It might be enough to say that Canada should not be deprived of the great advantage of having a representative in such a highly
The Address-Mr. Poulin accredited place. In support of this case, I shall quote the views of a member of this house who was then an ordinary representative-though, please the Lord, he was far from ordinary-and who is now a minister in the present government. Moreover, he is a man of superior intellect, in whom the government had the greatest confidence and who is therefore often entrusted with most delicate missions abroad. I mean the honourable minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and shall to this effect, quote an issue of The Ensign published in 1950.
(Text):
Canada is losing information by not having a diplomatic representative at the Vatican, says James Sinclair, parliamentary assistant to Finance Minister Abbott and Liberal member of parliament for Coast-Capilano, B.C. Mr. Sinclair expressed his views in a letter of support to a Catholic Women's League subdivision in Vancouver and to various Protestant groups who oppose the appointment.
Following is the text of Mr. Sinclair's letter:
The Catholic church is fighting communism wherever it exists, and it has no hesitation in accrediting representatives to even the communist governments, so that they may have all possible information. I met the Vatican's representative in Yugoslavia, and learned more from him - about the country than I did from any other diplomatic representative in Belgrade.
This, and other experiences, have led me to the belief that Canada is losing information by not having a diplomatic representative at the Vatican. Almost every European nation, Protestant and Catholic, has such representation.
In Canada, where we are comparatively new to the necessity for diplomatic representation, the problem has been discussed almost entirely on religious grounds, and if an appointment were made at this present time, a large proportion of our people would regard it as a religious appointment, and so be strongly opposed to it. Public discussion of this situation, however, will bring about a better understanding, which might eventually lead us to have a representation in the Vatican, as does Protestant England.
(Translation):
If the minister has changed his mind, I have no doubt that he will want to inform the house about it.
For those who closely follow international events, there is no doubt that the last three or four sovereigns of the Vatican were diplomats of a high order, dedicated to the welfare and happiness of peoples, irrespective of their religious beliefs. It should be noted those great leaders, fearless and blameless, have on many occasions condemned false or dangerous principles and denounced unjust or nefarious attitudes while carefully avoiding to direct their attacks against the countries or their leaders in particular.
What about the special qualities of the great statesman who, for the past 18 years, has been presiding over the destinies of that
278	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Poulin city? Severe and demanding when he, himself, is concerned, he is full of compassion and indulgence for others. Placed on neutral ground between two clans of opposite ideological concepts, he does not fear from time to time to raise his serene voice to tell the ones that atheism, under whatever form it appears, is a baneful doctrine for humanity and, to the others, that there can be no compromise with evil. In these troubled times, how gratifying it would be, not only to listen to that voice from the centre of St. Peter square, but also to hear its repercussions in the very sumptuous halls of NATO and UNO. To the list of the most influential statesmen of the world which the Prime Minister gave us in this house last Wednesday, the 9th of January, I would gladly add the name of His Holiness, Pope Pius XII, and I would even place it at the head of the list. One cannot help but have a deep feeling of admiration on reading the speech made by Pope Pius XII in September, 1954, on the problem of A.B.C. warfare, as well as his Christmas speech of 1955 on peace, not to mention the one he made last Christmas. Where, anywhere in the world, could one find a more enlightened, more objective, more sincere and disinterested propagandist? I can understand how, on March 1, 1955, the Ottawa Journal could write the following in its editorial page:

A Great Pope
Tomorrow in Rome Eugenio Pacelli, Pius XII, will observe his 79th birthday and his 16th year as Pope.	.
The whole free world, all at any rate in the tradition of Christian-Judaeo civilization, will send congratulations.
For Pius XII has been more than a great Pontiff of Rome: his character and moral and intellectual leadership have undoubtedly influenced all areas of the earth where spiritual values remain.
There are those who hold that Pope Pius has been the greatest Roman Pontiff since Gregory the Great. Certainly no other pope since the year when Leo went out to meet Atilla has faced more difficulties courageously, and none won more respect from men of different faiths.
"The Pope-how many divisions has he"? asked Stalin. Yet Stalin was to learn that spiritual and moral forces exist mightier in the long run than divisions of steel.
(Translation):
I cannot refrain from mentioning here a news item published in he Devoir of March 12, 1956, reporting a statement by senator Barkley, former vice-president of the United States, who had this to say about His Holiness Pope Pius XII:
I do not believe that there has been a greater force working for peace and democracy in the world than he has been.
Such testimonies tell us why the majority of the great statesmen of the world are proud


and honoured to visit him and seek his advice.
Indeed I have collected at random, in newspapers, a few pictures showing statesmen who seem proud and happy to have been photographed with our Holy Father the Pope on the occasion of a visit at the Vatican. For example, in the Montreal Gazette of April 11, 1956, there is a picture of none other than the secretary general of the United Nations Mr. Dag Hammarskjold, who is photographed with His Holiness Pope Pius XII. The legend read as follows:
(Text):
United Nations Secretary General Dag Hammarskjold visits Pope Pius XII at the Vatican during the diplomat's Rome stopover on the way to seek a peaceful settlement of Middle East hostilities. The Pontiff gave his blessing to Ham-marskj old's mission complicated by renewed Israel-Arab border fighting.
(Translation):
And at the bottom of another photograph reproduced in Le Droit of October 4, 1956, I read the following:
Received by the Holy Father: Senator Wishart McLea Robertson, Speaker of the Senate of Canada, and Mrs. Robertson, have been received on September 25, in a private audience granted by His Holiness Pope Pius XII, at his pontifical villa of Castelgandolfo.
Opinions have been expressed to the effect that the diplomatic channels that we are now using in our relations with the Vatican, that is the British embassy of Whitehall, were suitable and sufficient. Why should we proceed in such a way? Are we not a full grown nation since the statute of Westminster? Why allow a country which is our equal and our competitor in many fields, to look after our affairs while our prestige and our interests are at stake? If such a procedure is advisable in the case of the Vatican, it should also be proper in relation to the other countries. Let us then do away with our embassies, let us stop sending our ministers around the world, and let us limit their trips to visits to the British Isles.
Would it be a matter of money? If so, we certainly should remember that there are moral and spiritual values for which we are never paying too high a price, because they are priceless.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I would like the Anglo Protestant element of our population to realize, once and for all, that if the reiterated request for a representative of Canada to the Vatican is coming mainly from the Catholic and French province this does not mean that this province wants absolutely this representative to be a Catholic French Canadian.

We understand very well that this diplomat would represent Canada as a whole, as a country, and I would have no objection to his being either from French or English extraction, either Catholic or Protestant. He would only have to be a worthy citizen, well qualified, of irreproachable public character, and he should be able to do credit to our beautiful and great country, and to serve it well.
I would not like to conclude these few remarks without mentioning a matter, on which I have come back every year since I have had the advantage to sit in this house, I mean the raising of family allowances.
It would probably be appropriate to recall first of all that family allowances are and must remain an addition to family income. As a matter of fact, I believe this was the spirit of the legislation when it was voted in 1944. Nevertheless, this additional contribution was considered a minimum at that time, we are admittedly today far from this minimum, since to all practical purposes, the value of the dollar is scarcely more than half of what it was twelve years ago. My colleague for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) yesterday rightly called to our mind the essential part played by the family in the community.
On more than one occasion, in this house and elsewhere, I have attempted to establish the truth of the old saying "a community is only as good as the families in it". And if it is true that an individual needs to have a minimum of earthly goods to practise virtue, it is equally true that a family needs a minimum of revenue and adequate material conditions, for it is the source from which the individual must draw during the most important years of his life. The individual will never be but what his family made him.
I know that strong pressures are exerted in order that all social allowances be increased. It seems to me however that the case of families is more tragic and more urgent than all others. Indeed, if in the case of other assisted people difficulties due to the increase in the cost of living have increased twofold, these difficulties have been multiplied by 4, 6, 8 and even 10 on account of the number of children.
That is why it is most urgent to increase the rate of assistance in this field first, and to find out later what can be done in the other fields.
I urge therefore the hon. minister of National Health and Welfare and the government, to restore, during this session, the original value of this excellent social measure that was adopted in 1944, by doubling, or by increasing substantially the rate of family allowances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me congratulate the mover, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), and the seconder, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), on their excellent addresses made in reply to the speech from the throne. They certainly did a splendid job considering what they had to work with. I took particular notice of and listened very attentively to the remarks made by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. He gave an extremely vivid account of the growth of the city of Edmonton, and he may well be proud of the constituency he has the honour to represent. I believe it is one of the fastest growing cities in Canada, if not the fastest growing. Not only is it surrounded by a multitude of oil wells but it serves as a springboard for travel both by road and air to the far north.
I hope I am not yet too ancient, Mr. Speaker, but I can well remember visiting Edmonton with my parents in 1909. At that time Edmonton and Strathcona were separate towns and there were only two high level bridges crossing the river. One was the C.P.R. bridge and the other was for vehicles. Most crossings at that time were made by ferries pulled with a chain. I say again the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona can be justifiably proud of representing a riding which is an example for other Canadian cities to emulate.
I wish to express at this time how surprised and deeply grieved I was when informed of the resignation of Hon. George Drew, leader of the great national Conservative party. I am sure the contributions he has made here will be greatly missed, and the House of Commons will be the poorer for his absence. When we look back and realize the number of our colleagues in this house who have passed on in the not too distant past we are reminded again of the intense strain of public life.
Perhaps nothing could be more illustrative of this than the recent resignation of Sir Anthony Eden. Though criticized by many people in the past in his own country of Great Britain and within his own party, Sir Anthony has proven from time to time that he was right; and I believe when history is written the historians will agree that he was again right in regard to the Middle East. Perhaps it will not be long until the people of the free world will be slapping Sir Anthony on the back for the action he took in regard to the Suez crisis.

The Address-Mr. Stanton
Casting aside our personal thoughts or feelings, I think we must all admit that the action taken by the British and French governments in the Middle East has awakened the United Nations from a talking assembly, which no doubt it would have continued to be, to an active body truly representative of the free world. Too often in the past its members have sat idly by while the Russian communist regime spread its propaganda and influence all across the Middle East.
I am indeed happy, Mr. Speaker, to have as my leader at this time John Diefenbaker, a man who is internationally as well as nationally known, a man who enjoys the respect of nearly all the people of Canada, a man who has contributed much to the debates in this house and who will, I am sure, contribute much to government policy in future years, and I trust those years will extend far into the future.
This has been a very quiet session so far; indeed, how could it be otherwise? If you examine the throne speech mathematically it is obvious that nothing from nothing leaves nothing. It tells nothing of the past, offers no suggestions for the present and holds nothing for the future. Because the throne speech is so vague it is necessary for most hon. members to speak concerning the constituencies they represent, and I propose to do the same.
I am proud to be the representative of that grand old constituency of Leeds. On the south it is bounded by the great waterway of the St. Lawrence river, and contains within its boundaries all the Thousand islands. On the west and north it is bounded by the Rideau waterway. During the past summer I visited the St. Lawrence seaway development. It is tremendous in magnitude and the engineering skill involved is most wonderful, but I would like tonight to take the minds of my listeners back to the time when the Rideau waterway was constructed, between 1827 and 1832.
I believe it was a much more difficult task to construct the Rideau waterway than to build the St. Lawrence seaway. We must realize that the waterway was built by Colonel By through absolute wilderness. No means of communication of any kind had been established, and the project was completed in the unbelievably short period of six years. It was 123 miles in length and consisted of 47 locks. It may surprise some hon. members to know that this waterway cost only $2,500,000. This amount would barely cover the construction at Jones Falls today. Jones Falls is in my own constituency, and there is a dam there which is 60 feet

high. How was it constructed? They did not have derricks nor cranes. Those stones were put in place by hand labour. The canal was dug and constructed not with the modern steam shovels we have today, not with the huge tractor trailers that are now available, but by manual labour employing the wheelbarrow and the ox.
I speak of the Rideau waterway because approximately half its total length of 123 miles is in my constituency. I notice according to Hansard that some years ago certain hon. members of this house, who I am sure were not from eastern Ontario, seemed to be of the opinion that the Rideau canal should be discontinued. What a foolish idea. I may say that there are 53 lakes connected by the Rideau waterway located in the counties of Frontenac, Leeds and Lanark. This is a tremendous tourist attraction. You may talk about the Rocky mountains, Jasper park and so on, but I say to hon. members they should come down to Leeds county and they will see something practically as good for tired eyes to look at.
At this time I should like to deal with some of the problems we are facing in Brockville, my county town. During the past 15 years the population of Brockville has increased by 50 per cent. I feel that we are entitled to more consideration from the federal government, because we have had very little in past years. The population is 15,000 at the present time, with another 3,000 in the adjoining township which is in the process of being annexed. Yet we have a railway station which is not adequate in any sense for a town of that size.
The industrial development of the area is increasing by leaps and bounds. Parke Davis opened a large plant in the north of the city; Automatic Electric have increased their plant; Phillips Electric have increased their plant materially; Du Pont to the east have spent several millions of dollars and are planning another project which will cost in the neighbourhood of $8 million or $9 million. Surely we are entitled to more consideration.
Our post office is outdated, and federal offices are scattered all over the town. The excuse of the government for not starting and completing a federal building is that they want to wait until the town has been rezoned so they will know where to place the building. I may tell the house and the Minister of Public Works-I am sorry he is not in his seat-that the city has been rezoned, which rezoning has been approved by the municipal board. The city fathers are ready to cooperate with the government and the Department of Public Works. I am sure their representative would be welcomed by the

city council if he came down to lay out the work. I hope the minister will provide for this building in his estimates this session. Let us get on with the job. There is no excuse now that the city has been rezoned. Everything is in readiness for a start on the building.
I should like to say a few words in regard to our veterans. I listened to what the hon. member for Lanark had to say about some of these veterans. I believe he is right, as this is something which has been advocated by branches of the Legion across this country.
I agree with the submission that no veteran who served in Great Britain in the first world war for a year or more should be refused the same consideration as those who served in a theatre of war. It was through no fault of their own that these men did not see active service. They were held in Great Britain for other purposes. Their intentions when they enlisted were good, and they should receive the same consideration as other veterans.
I should like also to -bring up the question of veterans who have received aid under the Veterans' Land Act. There are very few of these veterans left. Some of these men have been paying on their mortgages for many years but have been unable to pay them off because of sickness and misfortune. Many of these men are in their late sixties or early seventies and, as I say, there are only a few of them left. Surely the department could now give them a clean sheet, a clear deed to their property, so that in the sunset of their lives they may live in peace without having this debt staring them in the face. Surely they have earned that consideration.
As far as old age pensions are concerned, it would appear that many government supporters are advocating an increase this session. If $40 a month is enough at the present time, then $40 a month was too much when the act was first put into force. If $40 was enough then, it is inadequate at the present time with the increased cost of living. Now that an increase has been advocated by many Liberal members I would not be surprised- I believe my colleagues agree with me-if the minister brought down an increase in old age security payments, this being an election year.
Then a word with regard to pensions for the blind. I know we all have sympathy for these people. Because of their blindness it costs these people more to live than it costs the average man or woman. I submit that they should have more consideration from the minister. They should be allowed to earn what they can without it interfering in any way with the small pensions they are receiving.
The Address-Mr. Stanton As for health insurance, we all know the stand this party takes on that. The Liberal party took their stand in 1919, and they have taken their stand again in every election since that time. Apparently after the election this matter goes unheeded. It would appear that the only way the people of Canada can receive any consideration in the matter of health insurance is to have a change of government.
As my constituency is 50 per cent rural I would be remiss in my duty if I did not take up this evening some of the problems that confront our farmers at the present time. We hear a great deal from members to our left concerning the problems of the west with respect to wheat, but I can assure the house that we have problems in the east. When the committee on agriculture met last session I was dismayed that the request of the concentrated milk producers to put their case before that committee was refused. The chairman of the committee said the terms of reference of the committee did not permit them to present their brief. The hon. member for Brant-Haldimand and I argued very strenuously that they should be permitted to present their brief on that occasion, but we were overruled. I know that some of the Liberal members who represent agricultural constituencies felt very keenly about the matter, but apparently because the problems of the concentrated milk producers did not pertain to wheat they were barred from entering the committee room.
There was an announcement in the speech from the throne of the setting up of a Senate committee to study the benefits that would be derived from an extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to include all Canada, so the residents of many submarginal farms might be moved to better locations where their incomes could be much increased. All I can say about the dairy farmers of eastern Ontario is that they are nearly all submarginal as far as their net income is concerned.
I have noticed that the Minister of Agriculture, together with many of his colleagues, has persistently said that the income of farmers has increased, but you never hear him say a word about net income. He never says a word about expenditure increasing much faster than the prices of the products that are produced. In fact the prices of the products produced have decreased very much since 1951 and 1952. During the war our farmers accepted the government's statements in good faith when they told the farmers to go easy, not to say a word then, to take what was offered them and the government would be good to them after the war. The farmers

The Address-Mr. Stanton of eastern Canada know just how good the government has been when it has allowed dairy products to come into our markets from New Zealand, and have not protected us from the actions of the United States.
You know, Mr. Speaker, our good friends to the south do not hesitate to impose tariffs, quotas and what have you when there is an overabundance of agricultural products in that country. But no, we must be friendly; we must be good children. We must accept everything they do and not make any reply whatsoever. I can tell you that our farmers are getting tired of the situation and fed up with the prices they are receiving at the present time. They are not being asked to move off their farms to better farms. In fact there are many 100, 200 and 300 acre farms in my own constituency at the present time, hundreds of them, where the land is lying idle. Why? Because many of these farmers can obtain higher remuneration by working in industrial plants. Many of them are getting too old to carry on their agricultural activities any longer, and with the present level of prices they cannot ask their sons to stay at home.
In my county, which traditionally has been a cheese producing district for many years, production decreased in 1955 by nearly 1 million pounds. Some may say that perhaps the milk has gone into other channels but that is not so, because one of our concentrated milk plants which enjoyed a patronage of around 800 a short time ago is now down to less than 500 patrons. Why? Simply because farms are idle. Most of the farmers are living on these farms because it would take all they would receive for their farms, machinery and cattle to buy a house in a town or city.
I was much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton when he spoke about the farm loan act. When that act was amended last year we were all hopeful that it would be easier for farmers and prospective buyers of farms to obtain more money on farm mortgages. I can assure you that it is hard for a farmer to borrow more money on a farm mortgage at the present time. Money which was formerly available to farmers by way of loans has completely dried up. Thirty or forty years ago people were looking for places to invest their money. That is not so today.
I cannot understand how it is that any person working in an industry, any civil servant or what have you, who is receiving a fair income, can borrow money on a home to the extent of 90 per cent of its appraised value while the farmer can only borrow up to 65 per cent, and even at that it seems to have been difficult for the farmer to do so 

during the past year. I have instances in my own constituency, just as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton has in his, in which loans on farms I knew were well worth far more than the appraised value were turned down by the farm loan board. Why I do not know.	.
The excuse has been offered to me that their revenue was not high enough. In some instances the money that farmers in my constituency were seeking was simply for the purpose of making their farms more remunerative. If the farm loan board officials and the government consider that a man working in industry with his two hands and who has no capital investment is a security risk much superior to the man with a farm worth $10,000 or $15,000 and having another $10,000 worth of cattle and equipment, there is something wrong and it is high time the government did something about it.
I am not going to take too long this evening, but during his speech the hon. member for Macleod made some prophecies regarding the Conservative party west of the great lakes. He made the prophecy that the Conservative party would come back after the next election with fewer members west of the great lakes than they have at the present time. With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few prophecies, and I do not believe that I will have to go too far out on the limb in doing so. I prophesy that the Social Credit party will not elect a member east of the Manitoba border, and that nearly all their candidates will lose their deposits. I will also make a prophecy that they will not elect a member east of the Alberta border. I am not saying that they will not do so west of that border, but I am sure their representation there will be decreased.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members of this house to the constituency of Prince Albert. Sir Wilfrid Laurier represented that famed constituency in the year 1896. Right Hon. Mackenzie King represented it in the years 1926, 1930, 1935 and 1940.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I associate myself with the previous speakers in congratulating

the mover and the seconder of the address in reply. The honourable members for Ed-monton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) and for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) made excellent speeches which justify the honour bestowed upon them by the Prime Minister and the members of the cabinet.
Then too, I should feel remiss if, at the beginning of my remarks, I failed to congratulate the new leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), for the confidence shown in him by the members and supporters of his party, and by reason of which he now bears the heavy responsibility of leading the forces of the official opposition in this house.
Under our parliamentary system we are allowed to disagree on the means of achieving the greatness of our country and the welfare of our fellow citizens. However the relations I have had with my colleagues in this house ever since I have come to it have been such as to convince me that each and everyone of us here, of whatever political persuasion he may be, is resolved to work towards the greatness of this country and to discharge his responsibilities to the best of his ability.
I would also like to avail myself of this opportunity, at the beginning of the new year, to offer my best wishes to all my colleagues and to the people of the constituency of Dollard, whom I have the honour to represent.
A great many of the opposition speakers who have spoken before me have stated that the speech from the throne read by His Excellency the Governor General of Canada at the opening of the session contained nothing or almost nothing. I cannot but think, when I hear that statement, that there are none so deaf as those who do not want to hear and none so blind as those who do not want to see. For my part, I have heard the speech from the throne in the other house and, later on, I took the trouble of reading it very carefully. I do not hesitate to say that this speech was very rich in proposals of national interest and that when its contents have been adopted by this house, it will promote an ever greater well-being for the population of Canada, ensure the maintenance of our economic and cultural development and be highly beneficial to the population which we represent. At the very beginning of the speech from the throne, we find that the government is eager to maintain the basic unity of the commonwealth and the reality of the western alliance. The Prime Minister, as well as the members of his cabinet, have proven and still prove to us that these words are not empty words. The close ties which link the Prime Minister to the prime minis-
The Address-Mr. Rouleau ters of the other member nations of the commonwealth, and the visits which have been exchanged during the last few years, and more particularly the last few weeks, when the prime minister of India came here to meet the Prime Minister of our country, prove this fact beyond the shadow of a doubt. While in certain cases they may have slight differences of opinion, they all agree on the goal which must be pursued by the association within the commonwealth. That goal is to safeguard the freedom of people, as well as the economic freedom of the member countries of the commonwealth.
The commonwealth association is made up of nations which are free, which enjoy full sovereignty, but have decided from their own free will, to unite in pursuing the goal I have just mentioned. The tour of Asia which the minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has just accomplished, is further evidence of the view I just stated, and I take this opportunity to offer hearty congratulations to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for having been such a good ambassador for our country, as well as an agent of peace and freedom for the commonwealth partnership.
The speech from the throne also mentions that Canadian military personnel is participating in the United Nations Emergency Force, which was suggested by Canada at the General Assembly of the United Nations, and here I would like, not only in my own name, but on behalf of my constituents of Dollard county, whose reaction was unanimous, to proffer our most sincere thanks and congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) who, at one of the most crucial moments for world peace, took upon himself to suggest what, to my mind, silenced the guns in the Middle East and prevented disaster from spreading to the whole world.
We remember with emotion that, when nearly everybody was saying that war was unavoidable, the Canadian representative at the United Nations devised a formula agreeable to all concerned, and that within a few days his suggestion had not only brought hostilities to an end in that part of the world but had removed the risk of another world war which had been hanging over us for several weeks. The Secretary of State for External Affairs had long been known as a great politician and a great diplomat, and he showed himself on that occasion the champion of peace.
At the very moment when trouble was brewing in the Middle East something still more terrible was happening behind the iron curtain, when a courageous and stout-hearted

The Address-Mr. Rouleau
people, in a united effort, decided to cast off for himself the needs of the refugees and con-the yoke of dictatorship, barbarism and sider the most appropriate and quickest way godlessness. This spontaneous gesture of a to help them and to facilitate their entry into freedom-loving people will have world-wide Canada.
consequences which can perhaps hardly be properly assessed at this time but will be felt perhaps sooner than we think. As mentioned in Time magazine of January 7, only later will it be possible to appraise the consequences of the action taken by the people. However the effects of this action on European politics and military forces are extraordinary. That people, unarmed and lacking practically everything, immobilized almost 80 Russian divisions, thus proving to the world that in a world-wide conflict the masters of the Kremlin cannot rely entirely upon an army reduced by them to slavery.
The action taken by the Hungarian people is the cause of all the waverings evidenced at the present time by the masters of the Kremlin. It also brought the world to the realization that the smiles by Khrushchev and Bulganin in the last few months were nothing but hypocrisy and humbug. By their barbarian military repression of this uprising for freedom on the part of the Hungarian people, the Russian communists and their leaders in particular have lost immense prestige throughout the world and among the partisans of the communist ideology. Thus since the barbarian repression of innocents with the help of Russian tanks, we have seen throughout the world thousands and thousands of communist militants leave the ranks of that movement. That action has also demonstrated that it is impossible for the Russian communist party to suppress liberty entirely and to brainwash youths to make them into machines of the state believing in no spiritual or moral values. That action equally demonstrated to the world that peoples and individuals have a deep-rooted need of truth that no method whatever can suppress and that is why all the nations of the world should be thankful to that people and should take every means possible to help those who left their family and their country to flee the vengeance of the masters of the communist party in the Kremlin.
The speech from the throne shows that Canada played its part and continues to do so to prove its gratitude to that people, by assisting through the Red Cross or otherwise those who still suffer in Hungary and the others who have come to establish themselves in our vast and rich country. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) went in person to Austria to see 
Already thousands of Hungarian refugees have reached our country and we shall welcome thousands of others in the near future. Each and every one of us in Canada who have enjoyed for generations living in a free and prosperous country, which has not experienced the anguish of war and the yoke of dictature, must warmly welcome those who so gallantly fought for the freedom and the safeguard of their faith.
When Christ came on earth, he taught us the great principle of love and charity. He urged us to practise charity, saying: "Love one another, give drink to those who thirst, and food to those who hunger." The Hungarian refugees who are coming to this country not only are our brothers, but they are also the champions of our way of life since they have fought for freedom, which we cherish so much. They are entitled to our respect, and I am convinced that, like the Canadian government, each and every one of the citizens of our country will take pleasure in welcoming them and assisting them. While I was speaking about the Hungarian refugees, I happened to mention our country which is so prosperous, so large, and so endowed with natural resources. The fact is even mentioned in the speech from the throne in these words. I quote:
Excellent progress is being made in our national economic development. Expansion is evident in every part of Canada . . . employment has reached unprecedented levels.
To sum up, Canadian production as well as national revenue are reaching unprecedented heights, a fact which is not without worrying the government because of the danger of inflation which seems to follow upon the overly rapid development we are undergoing. To overcome this danger of inflation which threatens to bring about serious economic consequences, the government is of the opinion that we continue to take some steps designed to check inflation by restricting credit in this country. It is because of this that I would like to make a request on behalf of my constituents from Dollard. In my constituency there are hundreds of industries and an even larger number of tradesmen and contractors, and I would like to ask the government to continue to protect them in every possible way. This protection is especially necessary to small tradesmen and manufacturers as a safeguard against calamitous inflation. I have no doubt that the members

of the Canadian government have no wish to see these people discontinue their activities and that they will see to it that necessary steps are taken to prevent them from undergoing too serious difficulties in the conduct of their business. In his speech on the address in reply, the leader of the opposition obviously made reference to the strike which was at that time paralysing one of the two large railways in this country, a strike which threatened to provoke serious trouble. However, instead of putting forward a solution, the leader of the opposition contented himself with saying, as is recorded in Hansard, volume 100, No. 3, page 26:
What does the government do? It continues its policy of being resolute in irresolution.
The Prime Minister answered then and I am quoting again from the same volume, page 36:
I can assure the hon. gentleman that my colleagues and I have not been inactive and that the remaining stumbling block has been narrowed very considerably.
Then the Prime Minister expressed what he believed to be acceptable to all, while not interfering with the democratic rights of each of the parties involved.
Time has shown that he was right as he was able to announce to the great satisfaction of the house and of the country that the strike had ended and that both parties to the dispute had accepted his proposal. In fact, one cannot more adequately express the feelings of the house and of Canada than was done by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) after the Prime Minister had announced the end of the strike, when he said:
We, too, express satisfaction that there has been no compulsion; free men in a free society, bargaining freely, have achieved the result. I am glad there was no compulsion exercised against either party in this dispute. I am sure the people of Canada will welcome the announcement made by the Prime Minister. I wish to congratulate all those who have participated in bringing about this satisfactory result.
If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who sits on the opposition side, saw fit to express such feelings I can, with all the more reason, sitting as I do on the government side, rejoice with the people of Canada which placed its confidence in the attitude of the Prime Minister throughout this crisis. I wish to congratulate him for his reasonable stand in the settlement of this strike and for the remarkable results he has achieved.
Through the voice of the governor general, the government has announced in the speech
The Address-Mr. Rouleau from the throne an amendment extending the scope of the Municipal Grants Act to authorize the payment of grants in lieu of taxes on federal property in all municipalities where such property receives normal municipal services.
I had the opportunity to read several editorials published by various papers throughout the country, and everybody will agree with me that the legislation was welcomed by the people and the municipalities who will benefit thereby. With the expansion experienced by most municipalities in the past few years, in the industrial, commercial and housing fields, the municipal councils had to face growing needs which had to be paid for in a short period of years. The municipalities had to build sewers, streets, sidewalks, and finally guarantee all the relevant services. Most municipalities who have known such developments have a real need of money and this measure announced by the government will greatly help the municipalities that have federal buildings on their territory. In the county which I have the honour to represent, and more particularly in the city of St. Laurent, the government has erected public buildings and I know that this legislation will be welcomed by the municipal authorities of this town which is one of the most progressive in this country.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to call attention to a part of the speech from the throne which, if it cannot but be of some concern for the Canadian people, is something to be enthusiastic over for a man of my generation who has the advantage of representing a county where the average age is young. I refer to the measure for the establishment of a Canada council for the arts, humanities and social sciences, which will certainly give a new impetus to the development of Canadian scholarship and culture.
Speaking of Canadian culture, I would like to mention an article published in the January 1957 issue of Esquire and written by one of the contributors to that magazine, Mr. Gerald Kersh. Like many others, I was surprised to read in that magazine, which usually gives good publicity to our country, that article by Mr. Kersh which suggests that an important part of the Canadian people, namely the French Canadians, have no culture and are all but uncivilized.
I would not mention it, if it was not that this magazine is read by millions of people, in Canada as well as in the United States.
28S

The Address-Mr. Rouleau I was told, too, that the manager of this magazine has apologized to the authorities of the province I. come from, and I appreciate it, but since these apologies have not been as widely publicized as the article, I fear that I would not be fulfilling my duty, not as a French Canadian, but as a Canadian, if X failed to call attention to this matter.
In his article, Mr. Kersh infers that we have no culture at all, that we Canadian citizens of French origin have produced nothing in the field of literature, music, painting or any other field. He holds also that, in the field of culinary art, the only dish that we have succeeded in inventing is pea-soup. He insinuates also that our language is very poor and he seems bent on describing us as a group of cave-dwellers. That article goes so far, Mr. Speaker, that when I started reading it I thought that it was a formidable joke; I thought that its author was trying to caricature us. If it is a joke, Mr. Speaker, it is in very bad taste, and if it is a caricature, it is badly done for it bears no resemblance to those it attempts to describe.
Mr. Kersh goes further and strikes at the very foundation of society, the family. He tells us that if we shut in for the winter a couple of Canadians of French origin, we shall find the following spring two or three little Canadians. Nothing could be viler. Our society, as I said, is based precisely on the family. Nothing is more sacred. I cannot understand a man like Mr. Kersh jeering at it. We are rightly proud of our large families. They constitute one of the greatest values and riches of the Canadian nation. When Mr. Kersh tells us that there is no cuisine in the province of Quebec, the facts belie that because it is recognized, not only throughout Canada, but also in the United States and even abroad that in the province of Quebec, and in the cities of Montreal and Quebec in particular, there are numerous places where dishes are the best and the most varied.
As regards our culture, it is easy to prove that, while we are a young nation, our culture is in full development. We are proud of the men the nation has produced in the fields of literature, arts, sciences or politics. Among the latter there are few Canadians more completely and thoroughly cultured than the present Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent whose mother was a great Canadian woman of Irish origin and whose father was a French Canadian. He was also so fortunate as to be brought up in Canada, in the province where I was born. At the beginning of my remarks concerning Mr. Kersh's article, I 

stated that I was moved to criticize these remarks which, to say the least, are quite unkind not so much because 1 am a Canadian of French origin but because I am a Canadian citizen. In attacking French culture he was also attacking Canadian culture since the people of Canada, even though its members may differ as to origin, and even though each group may have retained its own traditions, nonetheless forms one people. In spite of this diversity and because of it we have acquired a distinctly Canadian culture which, if it is allowed to come to fruition is called upon to be rich and to be capable not only of identifying a nation, but of serving it and of being also of service to the peoples of the world because of the development of our country and of the increasing influence which we wield in the councils of nations. It is up to us to enrich that purely Canadian culture in order to be worthy of our mission and so to be able fully to avail ourselves of the spiritual and even of the material values which Providence has dispensed to us. In that sense, I am firmly convinced that the bill for the establishment of a Canadian council for the arts, humanities and social sciences will mean an important progress. That is why I congratulate the Prime Minister who conceived this project as well as the members of the government for their contribution to its inception.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me particular pleasure at this time to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) on the brilliant manner in which he discharged his duty in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
(Translation):
I congratulate also the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the honourable member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). He has discharged himself of his task with a distinction which honours the constituency he represents, as well as his province. I have been much impressed by his remarks about higher education in Acadia. There will never be enough praise for the heroism of those who, until today, have been mainly responsible for the maintenance of the cause of the Acadians in their small country. Today, the federal government wants to increase its assistance to the Canadian universities. Our Acadian educational institutions will accept these grants from the government, confident that this new contribution will hasten in our part of the country a greater cultural development, and a wider influence of our Acadian ethnical group. The French fact in Canada

has a right to exist throughout the country. However, experience has shown that it is in the federal charter that the minorities of the country have most often found a guarantee of that right. Instead of considering the influence of a central government as a threat to their rights, the minorities have many times had cause to rejoice in having turned towards it. Such was the case for instance in connection with radio broadcasting. Such will be the case in connection with television. I am therefore happy at this time to congratulate this government for wanting to increase the grants to the universities of this country.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to point out the seriousness of the situation which until a few days ago was of great concern to all Canadians. By this I mean the strike which brought to a standstill the operations of one of our great railways. If it is true that this strike has now ended because of the spirit of co-operation shown by all interested parties, I believe that it is well to mention more particularly the conciliatory role played by the Prime Minister of Canada during these talks which brought about a solution to the strike.
I believe that all Canadians appreciate the outstanding part taken by the Prime Minister in these serious circumstances.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, it would be appropriate, I think, to mention here the satisfaction felt by all the members of this house at the return of the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). The message of good will which he has carried throughout the world, in the name of the people and of the government of Canada, will no doubt contribute to enhance, in the eyes of the other nations of the world, the already enviable prestige of Canada. We are therefore happy to express to the hon. minister our feeling of high appreciation for his distinguished services to his country.
I should also mention the part played by the hon. Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) who acted on behalf of our country in order to help the unfortunate Hungarian people. There was a humanitarian deed in the best Christian spirit. Canada has been enhanced by this action. The Canadian people must express all its gratitude to the man who represented this country so well in this circumstance.

On January 8 I was pleased to hear during the reading of the speech from the throne of the government's proposals to recommend in the Senate the establishment of a committee- ... to consider what should be done to make better use of land for agriculture and thus to
The Address-Mr. Michaud contribute more effectively to the improvement of agricultural production and the incomes of those engaged in it.
I know that all are conscious of the present condition, whereby farmers today are not receiving their proportionate share of the national revenue. I listened with interest the other day to the remarks made in this house by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, and I want to commend at this time the interest the hon. member has always shown in agriculture, particularly in regard to agricultural conditions in our own province of New Brunswick. At all times he has proven to be a strong advocate of more government assistance and support to New Brunswick farmers, and I have often shared his views in this respect. In his speech the other day, however, I felt the hon. member was being inconsistent when he took a critical view of the government's proposal to recommend the establishment of an agricultural study committee.
We are all aware that the farming population of our province, together with the farming population of the rest of the country, is not receiving an equitable return for its efforts. I am sure everyone, including the members of the government, will agree with the hon. member's contention that our farmers are hard-working people, that they are clever and no less backward than the rest of their fellow citizens, and that many of them are most successful in their undertakings; but we must not forget that agriculture is also a science and as such is open to a scientific approach in both the fields of production and marketing. I have no doubt that this is the thought the government has in mind when seeking plans which will assure our farming people a fair and equitable return for the job performed.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton further stated that what farmers in New Brunswick need is a market for their produce. I am quite in agreement with him on this matter, but might I be permitted to make another suggestion in this regard. Would not the readiest market available to maritime farmers be the maritime market itself? When we consider that we import between 60 and 65 per cent of the foodstuffs for our own local requirements this would appear to be the logical goal we should strive to achieve.
Pursuant to that matter I would like to express a view which I have already expressed in this house. This agriculture committee could properly seek ways and means to establish freezing and processing plants at points in farming areas, thus enabling the maritime farmers themselves to secure this ready market, for most of the food commodities we need can be produced at home.

The Address-Mr. Michaud
I am not of the opinion that the main source of our difficulties in relation to the maritime farm economy lies in the lack of soil fertility. I believe, on the contrary, that when properly cultivated our land is generally good, fertile land which can yield all the vital things we need for our own sustenance. 1 feel, therefore, there is a definite need for a committee such as was proposed in the speech from the throne on January 8, and I am looking forward with great hope that the task it will perform will mark a turning point in the farm economy of our country and more particularly in the maritime farm economy.
Again referring to the remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in this house last week, there is one point on which I might say that I am in some agreement with him. I am now speaking of his reference to the inefficiency of the Canadian farm loan board to cope fully with the credit needs of the Canadian farmers. There is a growing feeling of dissatisfaction toward the rigid attitude of this board in its appraisal of the credit requirements and actual assets of farm properties. It is no longer being considered by the majority of farmers as a farm loan institution, but merely as just another loan institution. Statistics could be produced to bear out that tendency. Between March 31, 1956, and December 31, 1956, the Canadian farm loan board received 64 applications from New Brunswick, 39 of which were approved, for a total of $149,700.
If we consider that farming is New Brunswick's chief industry, and if we also consider the number of farms in the province and the necessity of rehabilitating many of them, we must admit that these figures are not very impressive. I would suggest to the Department of Finance that they reconsider the terms and regulations now governing the operations of the Canadian farm loan board with a view to rendering them more flexible and more adequate to meet the requirements of those farmers who rely upon the facilities of this board for financial assistance.
However, we should not assume that the federal Department of Agriculture is solely responsible for the welfare of our farm population, and I would like to point out that under our constitution the welfare of our farmers is also the responsibility of the provincial authorities. In recognizing this responsibility I would hope that our provincial governments across Canada, including the government of New Brunswick, would realize they are not relieved of the responsibility of giving some assistance in matters of loan financing.
Referring to the fishing industry, I should like to say that in relation to the maritime

economy it is next in importance to the farming industry. In a general way I think it is right to say that our fishermen had a comparatively good year in 1956. This is particularly true of lobster fishermen, who form the majority of the fishermen in my own constituency of Kent. In this regard I should like to quote from a Moncton Times editorial dated December 8, 1956, concerning this matter:
Nature evidently beamed with favour on the lobster fishermen of New Brunswick during the respective open seasons around this province's coastlines in 1956. For this became known when the reports were submitted to the conference of federal fisheries officers just concluded in Moncton. "A decided increase" in the lobster catch is how district protection officer A. A. Robichaud summarized the over-all outcome of the various lobster-ing seasons this year.
For the fishermen of Westmorland and Kent counties, as well as others actively associated with or interested in this lucrative branch of the fisheries industry, the season, both in regard to catch and landed values, was one that again reflected increases. The crustaceans garnered from the fishing grounds in the Northumberland strait between Point Sapin, N.B., and River Phillip, N.S., totalled in volume 5,919,700 pounds and brought the fishermen a total revenue of $1,810,193.
This is the fourth successive year that an improvement in both catch and value has been recorded. It compared with the respective figures for 1955 of 5,299,000 pounds valued at $1,657,245; of those for 1954 of 3,067,700 pounds valued at $1,306,272, and those of 1953 of 4,133,200 pounds valued at $1,243,603.
And again:
From the standpoint of volume, it would appear that the stricter surveillance of the lobster grounds by augmented numbers of fisheries protection officers these past few years has had some effect in reducing the depredations of poachers as well as other illegal fishing methods. And the education program stressing conservation measures, which has been carried on during the past four years, has also had a beneficial effect in nurturing the valuable lobster population off the shores of this province.
The lobster fishery forms an important part of the economy of the eastern, northern and southern coastal areas of New Brunswick. It provides the fishermen with a considerable part of their annual income, and it is a matter of much satisfaction to see this increasing.
In my estimation that editorial gives a fairly comprehensive account of the situation inasmuch as it applies to the Kent county lobster industry. There seems to exist sufficient evidence of a healthful note of optimism for the future of that industry. Apart from that encouraging factor is also the prospect for many fishermen of unemployment insurance benefits which will become available next year to the fishing industry. This should prove of valuable assistance during the winter months, when the income of fishermen in my district is at its lowest level.
I was interested in reading on January 8 a press report stating that the Department of Fisheries plans to reseed the oyster fishing

grounds in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. In regard to this matter I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Moncton Transcript of January 10, and which very adequately sums up the situation. It relates the history of the disease which depleted our oyster grounds during the course of the past few years. It states:
In fact the experts have estimated that 90 per cent of the oyster stocks in the affected waters have been destroyed by natural mortalities over that comparatively short period of 1955 and 1956. This devastation, of course, caused not only a decided reduction in the volume of the shellfish garnered but also in the landed values.
The biologists found the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia oyster grounds had been swept by a disease similar to that which all but ruined the long-famed beds in Prince Edward Island between 35 and 40 years ago. So it is from the island's now prolific producing waters that disease-resistant bivalves will be transplanted to bring about the rehabilitation of the depleted oyster fishing grounds of the mainland provinces.
There seems no doubt but the method of rehabilitation will prove equally as successful in the present instances as was the case in restoring the Prince Edward Island beds some years ago. It will, of course, take several years before the process shall have completely eradicated the disease which has been depleting the oysters. In all, the plan will see 10,000 barrels of P.E.I. disease-resistant bivalves planted in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia
The Address-Mr. Michaud
fishing grounds over the ensuing three years, with the 1957 transplant totalling 1,500 barrels to be made in. May and June.
The federal government officials merit commendation in taking timely action towards the restoration of this fishery which in past years has been a valuable one to the fishermen of this and the other maritime provinces. Research has dictated that the oyster beds would rehabilitate themselves naturally within a period of 10 to 15 years, but the department's action gives recognition to the fact that it is unnecessary to deprive fishermen of this source of income for so long a period.
I wish to associate myself with the concluding words of that article, and also congratulate the Department of Fisheries for the active action being taken in this matter. I express the hope also that as a result of these activities we shall see the oyster beds of Kent county brought back to their former production which meant so much to the income of our local fishermen.
On motion of Mr. Weir the debate was adjourned.
